messages.body_plain:
Lies,
  I think that your question is hard to answer because it is not clear what you have in mind.  What would you like to plot on the x and y axes?

  Remember that the usual SEM residuals are residuals of the sufficient statistics (covariances, means), they are not individual residuals.  So, the resid method for lavaan objects will not give you and NxP matrix of residuals but rather a PxP matrix where N is the number of observations and P is the number of variables.

  Personally, I like to stem-and-leaf plot the unique off-diagonal residuals from the covariance matrix.  You might consider a scatterplot to plot these on the y axis and the observed values on the x axis.  Or, you could scatterplot standardized or normalized residuals against the raw residuals.

Keith

Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY

messages.body_plain:
Dear all

I am not used to SEM at all, but for the first time I think that is a great way to analyze my data from an experiment.

Here are the variables that I think should go into the model.

a) outcome: my dependent variable (binary)
b) treatment: my treatment variable (binary)
c) ssb: a latent that I cannot measure
d) exp1, exp2, exp3: three continuous measures that give me a hunch about ssb and so you would call them "manifest" I think.

Here are the relations that I think should go into the SEM.

1) treatment has an effect on exp1, exp2, exp3 and also on outcome.
2) exp1, exp2, exp3 manifest ssb.
3) ssb has an effect on outcome
4) exp1, exp2, exp3 are highly correlated

So I set up the following model:

# regressions
       outcome ~ ssb + treatment
       exp1 ~ treatment
       exp2 ~ treatment
       exp3 ~ treatment

# latent variable definitions
       ssb =~ treatment

# residual variances and covariances
       exp1 ~~ exp2
       exp1 ~~ exp3
       exp2 ~~ exp3

# intercepts

When I fit this model, I get two warning messages.

***
Warning messages:
1: In lav_data_full(data = data, group = group, cluster = cluster,  :
  lavaan WARNING: some observed variances are (at least) a factor 1000 times larger than others; use varTable(fit) to investigate
2: In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING: could not compute standard errors!
  lavaan NOTE: this may be a symptom that the model is not identified.
***

While the first message seems to be cause by the nature of the variables (binary variables having the small variances), I cannot wrap my head around the second warning message.

Do you have any clue on how to improve this model? Thanks for the help.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am conducting a longitudinal CFA. I am evaluating measurement invariance and when I restrict the factor loadings to be equal across time with estimator =  'MLM' (i.e. all missing values also deleted), I get the warning message that LV cov matrix is NPD.

Following advice from Terrence Jorgensen here: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/lavaan/V4ikmv6wGHE
I checked for the CI of the correlations of my Latent Variables. What I did was:

fit2 <- cfa(model = Model2, data = data, estimator = 'mlm', std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)
summary(fit2, ci = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

I indeed get some upper bounds that exceed 1.

Question 1: is it these upper bounds that exceed 1 why I get the warning? The largest upper bound is 1.023.
Question 2: in the configural model (without factor loadings fixed), I don't get this warning message. However, when I compute the CIs in the same way, I get e.g.: LV0 ~~ LV1 [0.921 ; 1.016]. Why doesn't it give me a warning here?
Question3: as soon as 1 CI upper bound of these LV correlations exceed 1, does that mean I should do something about my model? In other words, is the result of the model potentially wrong or unreliable?
Question4: Somewhat off topic here, but related to measurement invariance. I never see people checking if the residual correlations are still good when they proceed from one level to another when evaluating MI, should you only check e.g. the change in AIC, RMSEA, chi-square test, ... (i.e. overall GoF)?

Thanks in advance.

On Thursday, February 9, 2017 at 6:44:09 AM UTC-7, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > "The item not constrained will not participate in defining the factor mean difference" can you explain why?
>
> Latent variables are not observed, so we can only infer their distributional properties (means, variances) indirectly via their hypothesized effects on indicators.  We typically fix latent means for identification, but we can release those identification constraints (except for one group/occasion) when we constrain loadings and intercepts across groups/occasions.  When you constrain 5 out of 6 intercepts to equality, the differences in observed means of those 5 indicators between groups are assumed to be due only to differences in the common-factor means between groups. Because the 6th intercept is not constrained across groups, the observed means of the 6th indicator can differ not only because of common-factor mean differences, but also differences in the measurement parameters (intercepts).

Suggestions:

Use argument ordered="outcome". See http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html

Leave out the residual covariances at first. I think that having them between all three pairs of exp variables is likely to cause trouble.

Providing a reproducible example would make it easier for people to help you.

The configural and weak invariance are estimating without any problem. In the next steps 2 problems are occuring:

a) When I am trying to fix thresholds -  intercepts are estimated for both original latent variable (AVM) and phantom variable (AVMph), which they shouldn´t, right? Then I have 10 more free parameters in model with phantom variables in comparison to the same model but without phantom variables.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to understand how scaled chi square difference test in DWLS models is computed.

For example, if I test the measurement invariance between fit.configural and fit.loadings. The parameters are:
c1 = 1.459
c0 = 1.852
d1 = 734
d0 = 758
T1-DWLS= 1448.002 (robust = 1466.741)
T0-DWLS = 1601.482 (robust = 1360.415)

Lavaan gives me :

df-diff = 24
Chisq-diff = 11.0763
P(Chisq) = 0.9885

But if I try to compute myself Chisq-diff by using Satorra-Bentler method where:

cd = (d0 * c0 - d1*c1)/(d0 - d1)

df-diff = d0 - d1

Chisq-diff = (T0* c0 - T1*c1)/cd

Results are very different:

df-diff = 24
Chisq-diff = 61.52
P(Chisq) <=.001

The difference between Chi-squares is different but, essentially, the conclusions are totally opposite. If I use robust Chi-squares for computation, the difference is other but always p <=.001.

Does somebody know how lavaan computes the Chi-squares difference? Is it necessary to adjust the two Chi-squares before computation of the difference? If yes, how do that?

Thanks a lot for your help and best regards

Hclaude

Hello,

I ran into a puzzling outcome while using lavaan and hoped to get another perspective on the issue. I am new to lavaan, but have experience with path-analysis.

I constructed a simple model with observed variables: B causes both A and C (diagram below).
A, B, and C are the only variables in the model, and the only paths are B>A and B>C. No covariance between A and C is specified. This model should have 1 degree of freedom because the association between A and C is expected to be the product of paths B>A and B>C, which can be compared to the observed association to test model fit.

Although I believe I specified the model correctly, lavaan did not use the association between A and C to test model fit, rather, the output shows a model with 0 degrees of freedom. I am puzzled by this and wondering if someone with more experience could weigh in, or suggest better ways of using lavaan for path-analysis.

Thanks in advance for any help. Here is the code, the relevant output, and the diagram:

mod1 <-'
A ~ a1*B
C ~ a2*B

messages.body_plain:
The default behavior for the sem function is to covary residuals for endogenous variables (see the help file for the sem function ?sem for details). In particular the option auto.cov.y is set to true. To turn off this behavior you can set auto.cov.y=FALSE in the sem command, explicitly set the covariance of a and c to zero in the syntax, or use the lavaan function (which has fewer defaults).

Alex

messages.subject_clean: lavaan removing degree of freedom? (unspecified endogenous covariance)
messages.body_plain:
To add to Alex's answer, the default behaviour of the sem() function is to include residual covariances for endogenous variables that do not also appear on the right-hand side of a "~" in the model specification.

For example, if you had

mod2 <- '
A ~ B
C ~ B
D ~ A + C
'

then sem() would not automatically include A ~~ C.

The model you were trying to specify is

mod1 <-'
A ~ a1*B
C ~ a2*B

A ~~ 0*C
'

messages.subject_clean: Question regarding lavPredict
messages.body_plain:
On 03/20/2018 12:28 AM, David Kaplan wrote:
> the type="ov" command, and would like to know if lavPredict is
> estimating the observed variables using the full model with
> time-invariant predictors.

What lavPredict() does (when type="ov") is the following:

1) it predicts factorscores in the usual way: we compute a 'factor score
weights matrix' (say, 'FSC', based on the model matrices), and then we
get factor scores by computing Y %*% t(FSC) (where Y is the data).

2) next, when type = "ov", we simply multiply the factor scores by the
factor loadings to get values for all the indicators

This can be useful for diagnostics (and it is used when you ask for
case-wise residuals), but this was never intended for 'prediction'.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan group,

I am analysing a dataset that consists of host individuals and their parasite communities that I sampled in three different landscape types.

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-w4g_xGHWqoQ/WrUP28TRlqI/AAAAAAAAAbY/Rt9UKh9kR3gMXMA63-1ff6HW0LKfMQ2ZgCLcBGAs/s1600/studydesign.jpg>

I am interested in the effects of intrinsic (i.e. gender, genotype) and extrinsic variables (i.e. landscape type, host density, species diversity) on the infection status with a set of parasites. More precisely, some of the parasite species are for various reasons more relevant then others, so I would like to

1) predict the occurrence of specific parasites in the host species while taking into account the absence/presence of other parasites and

2) to investigate whether and which of the intrinsic and extrinsic variables predict parasite richness in host individuals.

This is a model based on my theoretical knowledge on the the study system:

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-F7uPur2eHcI/WrUPcW4WvmI/AAAAAAAAAbU/sRgMDAHRcrkY-svzv6r9MTv0oEC5TCxWwCLcBGAs/s1600/path_chart.jpg>

Here is my code:

#create dummy variables for all factors

data2=dummy.data.frame(data1)

# structured equations for lavaan

model1 = "#regressions

parasite1 ~landscapeB + landscapeC + genderMale + hostdensity + speciesdiversity

speciesdiversity ~ landscapeforest.fragment + landscapeisland

hostdensity ~ landscapeB + landscapeC + speciesdiversity

# covariances

parasite1 ~~ parasite2

parasite1 ~~ parasite3

parasite2 ~~ parasite3"

#fit model

model1.sem = sem(model1, data2, estimator = "WLSMV")

The output seems to make sense and the results for one parasite species are congruent with the results from an independent analysis using a glm.

However, I was wondering whether the input for the model is correct and if my data in general is adequate as input for lavaan.

My specific questions are the following:

1) I am unsure if I need to order the binary parasite data as recommended in the lavaan tutorial for categorical endogenous variables.

If I order the data with

data2[,c("parasite1",

              “parasite2”,

              “parasite3”)] <-lapply(data2[,c("parasite1",

                                                              “parasite2”,

                                                              “parasite3”)], ordered)

and fit the model I get the following error message:

Error in lav_data_full(data = data, group = group, cluster = cluster, :

lavaan ERROR: ordered variable(s) has/have only 1 level

2) Does the hierarchical structure of my data permit to draw conclusions from the lavaan output, since I cannot include e.g. a random effect of study site? I also tried Jon Lefcheck’s R package piecewiseSEM for this reason. However, I do not know how to retrieve inter parasite covariances from this analysis.

3) Is there a function in lavaan to visualize the summary output as a path diagramm?

Thank you for reading! Any help would be much appreciated!

Cheers,

Julian

  This is a very complex model.  (I hope you have a large sample.)  So, it is going to pose a challenge.  The strategy that I would recommend would be to break that challenge down into a series of smaller challenges.  You might try something like this.
1. Begin working with manually drawn diagrams so that you can work out presentation strategies by directly editing the diagram.
2. Break up the measurement and structural portions of the model and present them on separate diagrams, one presenting a CFA and the other presenting what is essentially a path diagram for the latent variables (using circles).
3. Consider whether it is necessary to represent the mean structures in the diagram.
4. Use smaller double-headed arrows for the residual variances and see if you can rotate them to a more optimal position around the variable  to which they point.
5. Once you have worked out the presentation issues for separate diagrams, see re-evaluate whether it makes sense to attempt a combined diagram.
6. Once you have worked out a manually drawn diagram to your satisfaction, then consider whether it makes sense to reproduce it using code instead of manual construction.

Keith

messages.subject: Re: How to get outliers for a selection of variables used in a SEM
messages.subject_clean: How to get outliers for a selection of variables used in a SEM
messages.body_plain:
Lies,
Again, this is not a lavaan question so much as a general SEMNET question.  That may be why it has gone unanswered.  Here is the code that I use in my data preparation lecture.  Substitute your own data frame for NSKK.df.  If I were writing the code today, I would probably use the head() function rather than indexing to print out just the first 20 cases.  However, that is more for illustration and to check for errors than it is a functional part of the analysis.

# These packages must be installed before loading.

require(psych)

require(moments)

require(robustbase)

require(MVN)

require(mnormt)

require(mi)

require(rela)

(snip)

# Multivariate Normality tests from package MVN

#  Useful to run all three because they are not equally sensitive.

Mardia.NSKK <- mardiaTest(NSKK.df)

Mardia.NSKK

Henze.Zirkler.NSKK <- hzTest(NSKK.df)

Henze.Zirkler.NSKK

Royston.NSKK <- roystonTest(NSKK.df)

Royston.NSKK

# MVN provides univariate tests and plots to follow up

uniPlot(NSKK.df, type='histogram')

uniNorm(NSKK.df, type='SW', desc=TRUE)

# Mahalanobis test (for multivariate outliers)

NSKK.chisq <- mahalanobis(

    x = NSKK.df,

    center = colMeans(NSKK.df),

    cov = cov(NSKK.df)

    )

NSKK.pvalue <- pchisq(q=NSKK.chisq, df=4, lower.tail=FALSE)

MahalanobisOut <- cbind(1:1000, NSKK.chisq, NSKK.pvalue)

# Only print first 20 cases.

MahalanobisOut[1:20,]

# View outliers only.

MahalanobisOut[MahalanobisOut[,3] < .05,]

#plot

par(ask=FALSE, mfrow=c(1,1))

hist(NSKK.chisq)

Critical.chisq <- qchisq(p=.05, df=4, lower.tail=FALSE)

abline(v=Critical.chisq,col='red')

text(x=Critical.chisq, y=400, labels='p < .05', col='red', pos=4)

# Robust Mahalanobis Distance

# Compute robust Mahalanobis distances

robMD <- covMcd(NSKK.df)

plot(NSKK.chisq, robMD$mah, pch=16,

  xlab='Standard Mahalanobis Distance',

  ylab='Robust Mahalanobis Distance')

abline(a=0, b=30, col=gray(.60))

# Compare robust and sample means

colMeans(NSKK.df)

robMD$center

# Compare SDs

sqrt(diag(cov(NSKK.df)))

sqrt(diag(robMD$cov))

# Compare correlations

round(cov2cor(cov(NSKK.df)),2)

round(cov2cor(robMD$cov),2)

# The centroid and covarianc matrix look very similar

# Nonetheless they make a big difference to the range of

#  Mahalanobis distances.

# Convenient plot & list

quan.NSKK <- mvOutlier(NSKK.df, method='quan')

head(quan.NSKK$outlier, 10)

tail(quan.NSKK$outlier, 10)

Julian,
  I cannot give you a complete answer but given that your question has not yet received a reply, here is a partial one.

1. I am not aware of a manner in which specifying a variable as ordered would alter the number of unique values.  It seems to me that univariate descriptives are the logical next step to investigate this error message.  The message is essentially saying that within the context of the analysis one of the ordinal variables is a constant.  This can sometimes result from patterns of missing data.
2. You can always do a fixed effects analysis.  This does not preclude interpretation but merely alters the interpretation.  Your analysis is specific to the higher-level units in the sample rather than treating them as a sample to be generalized to a larger population.
3. See the thread about plotting diagrams for more on this topic.  The following package may be useful to you.  However, if you are looking fore AMOS like output with the estimates displayed, I am not aware of a tool for that.

messages.subject: Re: Measurement invariance - phantom variables and residuals fixing
messages.subject_clean: Measurement invariance - phantom variables and residuals fixing
messages.body_plain:
Aneta,
  If I follow your question correctly, you are using the theta parameterization for ordinal variables and want to compare a model with loadings and thresholds constrained to equality across groups to a second model which further constrains the residuals to be equal.  My understanding is that this refers to the residuals on the latent continuous variables that underly the ordered observed variables.  Further, the distinguishing feature of the theta parameterization is that it fixes these residual variances to unity.  As a result, constraining them to equality will add no further constraints to the model.  That is why your degrees of freedom do not change.

  I am not sure what you mean by fixing thresholds.  The group.equal parameter imposes equality constraints across groups but does not fix the parameters.  These are free parameters in both the theta and delta parameterizaitons.

  If that does not answer your questions, then my suggestion would be to work out a minimally sufficient example to illustrate the problem that you are trying to solve.  Also, questions about measurement invariance with ordered variables are quite frequent in this forum.  So, you can find discussion of best practices with references by searching related threads.

Keith

Some additional information:
- sample size: 924
- Likert scales were used, so it seems to me that outliers can't be the problem
- data is not distributed normally, therefore I used MLM as estimator

Thanks in advance!

messages.subject_clean: Question about Polychoric correlation and p-value of RMSEA
messages.body_plain:
Greeting,

I have a dataset with about 1200 complete subjects. There are 23 manifested indicators in my dataset, all of those indicators are 4-point Likert like scale.
After a long self studied, I think that I should use polychoric correlation instead of Pearson's correlation (due to ordinal scale of manifest indicators)
I used R and ran EFA using psych package which suggest 6 factors. I specified the model and cfa command in lavaan as followed...

model <- 'F1 =~ x1+x2+x3+x4
                F2 =~ x5+x6+x7
                F3 =~ x8+x9
                F4 =~ x10+x11+x12+x13
                F5 =~ x14+x15+x16+x17
                F6 =~ x18+x19+x20+x21+x22+x23'
fit <- cfa(model, data=data,std.lv <http://std.lv>=T, ordered = names(data), estimator = 'wlsmv')

The robusted fit indicator for RMSEA(90%CI) and p-value are 0.065, (0.062 - 0.069), and 0.000
However, when I removed the 'ordered' part from my command p-value for RMSEA changed to 0.860.
I tried to adjust the model using modnidices which improved fit indicators for a bit, but the effect of 'ordered' is still the same (i.e., p-value changed from highly significant to unsignficant)

I would like to ask for suggestion if statistical significant of RMSEA p-value is the effect of polychoric correlation (which I guess it markedly change the correlation matrix from the data) or if my cfa command is incorrect.

Best,
Wisarut

messages.body_plain:
It is quite possible. Look at the two correlation matrices--the Pearson and the polychoric. They may be substantially different. Crude ategorization of observed variables can attenuate correlations, and the weaker correlations can reduce power, making fit seem less bad. If that is true in your case, then the Pearson-based results are untrustworthy. You might also look at the bivariate distribution of observed responses. The polychoric correlation presumes that there are underlying bivariate normal responses. If the bivariate distributions seem inconsistent with such an assumption, then the polychoric-based results may also be dubious.

Did you use the same WLSMV estimator in both cases? If you changed estimator, that might also have an efect on your results. Alternately, with lavaan, the combination of ordered + WLSMV may mean something substantially different from the combination of continuous + WLSMV.

messages.body_plain:
Nicolas--
When you create the slope as a factor, you turn a model parameter into a variable. Then this variable must have a variance, which is differences in the value of the slope across respondents. A fixed coefficient slope model is one where there is no variation in slope across respondents. But if there is 0 variance in the slope coefficient, then it can't be used to predict dependent variables. So you might try simply deleting the slope factor from your model.

I admit, I don't know how to use lavaan to specify a model with random intercept and nonrandom, nonzero slope. Sorry.
--Ed Rigdon

> Does fitMeasures(fit = myfit_with_MLM, baseline.model = null_model_with_MLM) compute the robust goodness of fit indices based on the robust statistics of the specified null model?

Yes, that is correct.  If lavaan sees that you passed a lavaan object to the baseline.model= argument, it will use that instead of fitting the default independence model.

> The null model has a baseline.chi.square.scaling.factor of 1.208 (and chisq.scaling factor of 1.058), while "my_fit_with_MLM" has a baseline.chisq.scaling.factor of 1.058 (and chisq.scaling.factor of 1.135). I am somewhat confused by this

Me too.  Whenever I fit my custom null model to the same data with the same arguments, the baseline.chisq.scaling.factor is the same for both my null model and my hypothesized model, because in either case, lavaan fits the same default baseline model to calculate any requested incremental fit indices.

library(lavaan)
example(cfa)
fitMeasures(update(fit, estimator = "MLM"))["baseline.chisq.scaling.factor"] # 1.164138
## custom null model
mod.null <- paste0("x", 1:9, " ~~ foo*x", 1:9)
cat(mod.null, sep = "\n") # more restricted than independence model
fitMeasures(update(fit, model = mod.null, estimator = "MLM"))["baseline.chisq.scaling.factor"] # 1.164138

> Do you know how I can plot (scatterplots) these standardized residual matrixes in R?

Plot what against what?  If you are comparing the correlation residuals between 2 competing models:

example(cfa)
mod.null <- paste0("x", 1:9, " ~~ foo*x", 1:9)

(myResiduals1 <- resid(fit, type = "cor"))

uniqueCorResids0 <- myResiduals0$cor[lower.tri(myResiduals0$cor)]
plot(x = uniqueCorResids0, y = uniqueCorResids1, xlim = c(-1, 1), ylim = c(-1, 1),
      xlab = "Null Model", ylab = "Target Model", main = "Competing Model Residuals")
abline(h = 0, v = 0, lty = "dotted", col = "grey69")

If you want to visualize the residuals of a single model as differences between observed and model-implied covariances:

example(cfa)
(impliedCor <- lavInspect(fit, "cor.ov"))
impliedVec <- impliedCor [lower.tri(impliedCor )]
(observedCov <- lavInspect(fit, "sampstat"))
observedCor <- cov2cor(observedCov$cov)
observedVec <- observedCor[lower.tri(observedCor)]
plot(x = impliedVec , y = observedVec, xlim = c(-1, 1), ylim = c(-1, 1),
     main = "Observed vs. Expected Correlations",
     xlab = "Model-Implied", ylab = "Observed")
abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = "dotted", col = "grey69")

messages.subject_clean: lavaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite
messages.body_plain:
> I indeed get some upper bounds that exceed 1.

If your point estimate already exceeds 1, then of course your upper confidence limit will exceed 1.  The relevant issue is whether your entire confidence interval includes plausible values.  Is your lower bound below 1?

> Question 1: is it these upper bounds that exceed 1 why I get the warning? The largest upper bound is 1.023.

No, the warning is only issued when the point estimates yield a NPD matrix (whether that is due to a Heywood case like yours or not).

> Question 2: in the configural model (without factor loadings fixed), I don't get this warning message. However, when I compute the CIs in the same way, I get e.g.: LV0 ~~ LV1 [0.921 ; 1.016]. Why doesn't it give me a warning here?

Because the point estimates imply a positive-definite matrix.

> Question3: as soon as 1 CI upper bound of these LV correlations exceed 1, does that mean I should do something about my model? In other words, is the result of the model potentially wrong or unreliable?

Not if it is consistent with sampling error.  But pay attention to model fit as well.  Gross model misspecification can cause this issue, but in my experience, that misspecification has to be pretty severe to cause Heywood cases, whereas Heywood cases are quite common in small samples like yours.

> Question4: Somewhat off topic here, but related to measurement invariance. I never see people checking if the residual correlations are still good when they proceed from one level to another when evaluating MI, should you only check e.g. the change in AIC, RMSEA, chi-square test, ... (i.e. overall GoF)?

I think I answered your question on SEMNET already :-)

messages.subject: Model specification: Connecting indicators with other variables in the model
messages.subject_clean: Model specification: Connecting indicators with other variables in the model
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have a small question about model specification. I specified a SEM model based on theoretical connections among the variables (two latent variables, with three indicators each, plus three observed variables). After this specification, fitting measures were acceptable. After analysing modification indices, I observed that by adding two correlations in the model, the fitting was much improved, indicating really good fitting to the data.

My question is about these two correlations. They can be written in the form: D ~~ X1; D ~~ Y1, where D is a dummy variable (ordered, not indicator), and X1 and Y1 are indicators of two different latent variables, say X and Y. Regressions between D and X, and D and Y are nonsignificant. Theoretically, the following relations are meaningful: D ~ X1 and Y1 ~ D, and so, I would prefer to have these two regressions instead of the corresponding correlations. However, after replacing the two correlations by these two regressions, I got an error due to D ~ X1 (but not from Y1 ~ D).

First question: Since I have never seen SEM models where indicators are connected with "exterior" variables of the model, I would like to know if the model including "D ~~ X1; Y1 ~ D" (correlation + regression) is well specified/ statistically meaningful. If not, what about including "D ~~ X1; D ~~ Y1" (correlation + correlation)? Notice that in lavaan both cases are allowed and converge.

Second question: Although it is a general SEM question, I would be grateful if you can tell me why is it senseless to specify the regression D ~  X1.

Best regards,
 csm

messages.subject: Re: Multi-group Confirmatory Factor Analysis, with mumtiple groupings and mixed numeric-ordinal items
messages.subject_clean: Multi-group Confirmatory Factor Analysis, with mumtiple groupings and mixed numeric-ordinal items
messages.body_plain:
Dear Dr. Terrence Johnson,

Following your advice, I tried to implement a sequence of invariance tests for ordinal (or mixed continuous-ordinal) items based on the paper by Wu & Estabrook, in the suggested order, trying to implement the corresponding equations in the papers' sections. I first produced a parameter table “as close as possible to the desired level” via “cfa” with “do.fit = FALSE”. Then, using the auxiliary functions for freeing and fixing parameters and imposing constraints in “measurementInvarianceCat” by Sunthud Pornprasertmanit, Yves Rosseel and you, I released/fixed the desired parameters. Finally, I computed each solution with a call with the parTable instead of the model with “do.fit = TRUE”. I examined the parameter tables and tested the method with a simplified model with a single factor measured by four ordinal items (V30, V31, V32, and V33, all related to afterlife beliefs). In the configural model, I compared the MYT parameterization with the lavaan::cfa defaults. The difference is that in the latter the scales of the latent response variables are identified independently for all groups (as if they were reference), whereas in the former the scales for non-reference groups are picked from the reference group via the constrained thresholds. Both parameterizations yielded the same fit measures, so I used the lavaan::cfa default.

Here is my code, for a single factor two-group (female, male) model:

# ===============================================================================================

> free.intercepts.fix.means <- function(pt,ngroups,intercepts.to.free,means.to.fix) {

+   for(var in intercepts.to.free) pt <- freeParTable(pt,var,"~1","",2:ngroups,NA)

+   #for(var in residuals.to.free) pt <- freeParTable(pt,var,"~~","",2:ngroups,NA) # lavaan default

+   for (fact in means.to.fix) pt <- fixParTable(pt,fact,"~1","",2:ngroups,0)

+   return(pt)

+ }

>

> fix.all.intercepts <- function(pt,ngroups,intercepts.to.fix) {

+   for (group in 1:ngroups) {

+     for(var in intercepts.to.fix) {

+       pt <- fixParTable(pt,var,"~1","",group,0)

+     }

+   }

+   return(pt)

+ }

> # ===============================================================================================

>

>

> # PART I - LOAD THE DATA FRAME, SELECT FACTOR ITEMS AND GROUPS

> # ============================================================

> religion <- get(load("../ISSP_CFA_Christian_And_Unaffiliated_Data_Frame.RData"))

> source("../lavaanParTable.R") # Auxiliary functions freeParTable, fixParTable

>

> # THESE ARE THE ITEMS FOR ALL FACTORS EXAMINED FOR RELIABILITY IN EFA:

> cfa.selected.items <- c("V14","V15","V28","V29","V30","V31","V32","V33","V35","V37",

+                         "V46","V47","V48","V49","V51","ATTEND")

>

> # THESE ARE THE SOCIODEMOGRAPHIC VARIABLES (GROUPINGS) FOR MGCFA ANALYSIS:

> cfa.groups <- c("AGE","MARITAL","SEX","DEGREE","WRKST","RELIGGRP","COUNTRY.NAME <http://COUNTRY.NAME>")

> religion <- religion[, c(cfa.selected.items,cfa.groups)]

>

> # CONVERT ITEMS IN DATA FRAME TO "NUMERIC"

> for (i in 1:length(cfa.selected.items)) religion[,i] <- as.numeric(religion[,i])

>

> # PART II - SPECIFY THE MODEL(s) AND COMPUTE MEASUREMENT INVARIANCE

> # =================================================================

> # DECLARE ORDINAL ITEMS; ALL OTHER ITEMS ARE TREATED AS NUMERIC

> ordered.items <- c("V30","V31","V32","V33","V35","V37")

>

> # SPECIFY THE MODEL

> model <- 'afterlife.beliefs   =~ V30 + V31 + V32 + V33

+          '

>

> fit.indices <- c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "cfi",

+                  "rmsea", "rmsea.ci.lower", "rmsea.ci.upper",

+                  "srmr", "pgfi", "pnfi")

>

> # TEST FOR "SEX"

> # ==============

> # CONFIGURAL MODEL (LAVAAN DEFAULTS, EACH GROUP IDENTIFIED INDEPENDENTLY)

> configural.SEX <- cfa(data = religion[-which(is.na <http://is.na>(religion$SEX)),], model = model,

+                              ordered = ordered.items,

+                              group = "SEX", group.equal = "",

+                              estimator = "WLSMV",

+                              parameterization = "theta", do.fit = TRUE)

>

> # Number of groups, variable and factor names for invariance tests

> ngroups <- max(partable(configural.SEX)$group)

> intercepts.to.free <- c("V30","V31","V32","V33")

> intercepts.to.fix <- intercepts.to.free

> the problem was apparently caused by the data on one specific parasite species that was only present in two out of three landscape categories  (which are predictors of the parasites presence/absence). I added an artificial data point (i.e. an infected individual) to the landscape where no infected individuals were caught and fitted the model again. This time the model converged without problems.
> Is there a way to make my model converge without introducing an artificial data point?

Was it the reference landscape in which one of the outcomes was a constant (always 0 = absent), or was it one of the landscapes indicated by one of the 2 dummy codes?  If it was in a dummy-coded landscape, you can leave that dummy code out of the regression equation for that particular outcome (or equivalently, set that slope to zero: DV ~ 0*dummy) -- this will not affect the interpretability of the other slope.

If it was the reference category, you could still include both dummy codes as predictors, but there is nothing for them to be "in reference" to.  With linear regression, you could identify your model by fixing the intercept to zero for that outcome, essentially turning the slopes of each dummy code into a group-specific intercept instead of a group-specific deviation from the intercept.  You could do that here to, but since it is SEM software designed with factor models in mind, the tradition has been to fix intercepts to zero anyway and estimate thresholds.  But with binary outcomes, they are equivalent: intercept = -1*threshold, so you fix either to zero to get an equivalent model.  Long story short (too late), you can fix your threshold to zero for this outcome variable to identify your model: DV | 0*th1

messages.body_plain:
> In Mplus, you can use sampling weights to compute standard errors and the chi-square test statistic to account for clustered data. Is there a similar function in lavaan for ordered categorical data with WLSMV estimation?

The survey package can adjust for clustering, stratification, and sampling weights, and the lavaan.survey package provides an easy way to pass information to/from the lavaan and survey packages to get robust SEs for your SEMs.  Unfortunately, the survey package does not provide the tools to deal with categorical outcomes.

How many categories are there?  Some research indicates robust MLE  (e.g., estimator = "MLM") should yield sufficiently unbiased results when there are at least 5-7 categories, depending on how asymmetric the thresholds are.  But they only investigated regular CFA, not multilevel CFA.

http://psych.colorado.edu/~willcutt/pdfs/Rhemtulla_2012.pdf

If you have several items per factor, parceling would also be provide a way to items with more categories and therefore more likely for MLE to work.  But I do not recommend parceling if your research questions are about the measurement model itself.  Even if your research questions are about the structural level, you should take great care in how you allocate items to parcels in a theory-driven way:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3909043/

or to take uncertainty into account if you allocate parcels randomly.  See the references on the ?parcelAllocation help page in the semTools package for more information.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

> when I run the model in lavaan, I get a Rsquared for the Y-model that is through the roof (0.975 vs. 0.2725 in SPSS).

Which pseudo-R-squared does SPSS report for a logistic regression?  There are numerous proposed:

https://stats.idre.ucla.edu/other/mult-pkg/faq/general/faq-what-are-pseudo-r-squareds/

I also like Tjur's, not shown in the link above:

https://statisticalhorizons.com/r2logistic

lavaan runs probit regression with DWLS estimation, which starts by estimating polychoric correlations among the variables (treating your interaction as a separate variable, by the way).  So lavaan's R-squared is the proportion of latent-response variance that is explained by the predictors.  That could be quite different than pseudo-R-squared based on proportions or on log-likelihoods of target vs. empty models.

messages.body_plain:
> First question: Since I have never seen SEM models where indicators are connected with "exterior" variables of the model, I would like to know if the model including "D ~~ X1; Y1 ~ D" (correlation + regression) is well specified/ statistically meaningful. If not, what about including "D ~~ X1; D ~~ Y1" (correlation + correlation)? Notice that in lavaan both cases are allowed and converge.
>
> Second question: Although it is a general SEM question, I would be grateful if you can tell me why is it senseless to specify the regression D ~  X1.

You are almost specifying a well-known class of models called MIMIC models, which can be used to test for measurement equivalence/invariance (i.e., measurement parameters do not depend on D) and differential item functioning (DIF; i.e., whether a particular indicator's measurement parameter(s) do(es) differ across levels of D).  Here is an example application:

https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10862-008-9118-9

Essentially, yes, you can regress X1 and Y1 on D to test the relationships you theoretically expect.  But you also regress indicators (e.g., one at a time, or maximum all but 1 indicator so the model will be identified) on D to test for DIF.  Note, you regress indicators on D, you do not simply correlate them with D.  That way, factor loadings are estimated as the effect of the factor on the indicator, controlling for the effect of D.  If the effect of D on an item is substantial/significant (i.e., that item has "uniform DIF"), you need to make sure that estimate is in your model in order for the effect of D on the latent factor to be unbiased.  If none of them are, then you can leave the direct effects of D on indicators fixed to zero, and conclude scalar/strong invariance.

I have an upcoming book chapter I can share that shows how to test this in lavaan, as well as whether D and the latent factor interact to effect the indicator (i.e., to test metric/weak invariance).  I can email a copy if you write me a private email.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: Multi-group Confirmatory Factor Analysis, with mumtiple groupings and mixed numeric-ordinal items
messages.body_plain:
> Dear Dr. Terrence Johnson,

Jorgensen :-)  Terrence is fine.

> I first produced a parameter table “as close as possible to the desired level” via “cfa” with “do.fit = FALSE”.

I appreciate starting with a simpler, 1-factor model as an example.  May I also suggest starting with 2 groups before expanding to 26?

I also understand why you want to automate this in some way, given you have 26 groups, which would make the syntax quite hard to specify manually.  However, the hidden semTools functions (freeParTable, fixParTable) are not keeping up to date with the changes to the parameter table that lavaan specifies.  Eventually, I will phase those out.  I also recommend not relying on them when asking for help here, because it limits who can/will offer help.

You can still automate using the paste() function.  For example, here is how you can specify the parameter labels for factor loadings of one item (start small, then work up):

V <- 31 # variable 31
G <- 1:3 # 3 groups, for proof-of-concept
(parLabels <- paste0("L", V, ".g", G, collapse = ", ")) # "L31.g1, L31.g2, L31.g3"
paste0("F1 =~ c(", parLabels, ")*V", V)
[1] "F1 =~ c(L31.g1, L31.g2, L31.g3)*V31"

Capitalizing on the fact that you can pass a vector of character strings as the lavaan model (rather than everything in a single pair of quotation marks), you can loop through variables to create your model:

model <- character(0)
for (V in 30:33) {
  parLabels <- paste0("L", V, ".g", G, collapse = ", ")
  model <- c(model, paste0("F1 =~ c(", parLabels, ")*V", V))
}
cat(model, sep = "\n")
F1 =~ c(L30.g1, L30.g2, L30.g3)*V30
F1 =~ c(L31.g1, L31.g2, L31.g3)*V31
F1 =~ c(L32.g1, L32.g2, L32.g3)*V32
F1 =~ c(L33.g1, L33.g2, L33.g3)*V33

Then it is easy enough to scale up by setting G <- 1:26, and to loop over another set of V variables to define a different factor, and simply add that to the vector to make a larger model.  It is also simple to adjust what is being pasted to define different parameters ("~~" and "~1").

To equality-constrain parameters across groups, give them the same labels across groups (i.e., get rid of the ".g", G differences in the labels) by repeating the same label with the rep() function.  To make equal loadings:

model <- character(0)
for (V in 30:33) {
  parLabels <- paste0("L", rep(V, length(G)), collapse = ", ")
  model <- c(model, paste0("F1 =~ c(", parLabels, ")*V", V))
}
cat(model, sep = "\n")
F1 =~ c(L30, L30, L30)*V30
F1 =~ c(L31, L31, L31)*V31
F1 =~ c(L32, L32, L32)*V32
F1 =~ c(L33, L33, L33)*V33

Again, same principal applies for specifying other types of parameters.  If you are going to need to ask for help (understandable, given how complex this is, and too new to expect tutorial applications yet), I would recommend this because it makes easily reproducible syntax by any reader, and it gives you a way to check your model specifications visually in a way that is probably easier than inspecting a parameter table with so many rows.

> In the configural model, I compared the MYT parameterization with the lavaan::cfa defaults. The difference is that in the latter the scales of the latent response variables are identified independently for all groups (as if they were reference), whereas in the former the scales for non-reference groups are picked from the reference group via the constrained thresholds. Both parameterizations yielded the same fit measures, so I used the lavaan::cfa default.

That is what I recommend.  As the article shows, the models are equivalent, but lavaan's (actually, R's) optimizer has trouble sometimes with the MYT parameterization.  You seem to want to test equivalence of residual variances, so make sure to set parameterization = "theta" rather than the default "delta".

> The results look coherent.

I would very carefully count the number of parameters you fix and free between each step (configural to thresholds, thresholds to loadings, etc.), so that you can verify that you gain as many df as you expect.

> - In the original paper the factor variance-covariance matrix is set to I for all groups, but in my case I guess this is replaced by the marker item loading providing the scale;

Is MYT the "original"?  They estimated the factor covariance matrix and fixed a loading.  I do not recommend using a marker variable, because it biases subsequent tests of which item(s) has/have DIF, assuming a particular level of invariance is rejected.

> -          - I’m not sure the condition for fixing group means (kappa^(g) = 0 in the Wu & Estabrook paper) via fixing “~1” for the factor is correct. I found that the group means are only free and comparable for the scalar and strict levels (which seems correct);

That is correct.  Fix latent means to zero in all groups, until you constrain intercepts to equality, in which case only 1 group's mean has to be fixed to zero.

> -          - For the scalar and strict levels the thresholds are invariant, so they could be picked from the first group. But fixing them explicitly reduced the number of df and slightly changed the fit measures. I think this was done correctly.

You don't fix them, you just equality-constrain the estimates.  They don't belong to any one group, they are simultaneously the estimates for all groups.

> This seems to be working for this single factor model. I managed to compute invariance tables for 26 countries without convergence problems. But when I stepped to the three-factor model in the previous post (with marker items chosen by default) and tested for AGE, I got the following error:

To narrow it down further, try fitting 1-factor models for each factor, to see where the problem is before trying a 3-factor model.  If all three 1-factor models converge, then the 3-factor model might just be too large for the optimizer to handle.  The gradient is the first derivate of the vector of model parameters, and it tells the optimizer how to update the estimates in the next iteration.  So if the gradient cannot be calculated, convergence can't happen because the optimizer just doesn't know where to look for the solution.

Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

A slope is an effect size, and the standardized slope is a standardized measure of effect size (albeit questionable because sample-specific statistics are used to "standardize", so they may not map onto population parameters). messages.subject_clean: Multi-group Confirmatory Factor Analysis, with mumtiple groupings and mixed numeric-ordinal items
messages.body_plain:
> I would have to fix the factor variances in the model and use std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, and see if this leads to more convergence issues.

When you use that argument to fix the latent variances to 1, make sure you specify in the model syntax that all but the first group's variance is free when loadings are constrained to equality.  In a 2-group example, use NA to say that the value should be estimated for group 2:

F1 ~~ c(1, NA)*F1

This corresponds to the diag(Phi) column in Wu & Estabrook's tables (which are easier to interpret if you standardize the common factor and estimate all the loadings).

> I think I cannot test each factor separately because in the 3 factor model there are only 3 items per factor

3 items per factor is a just-identified model, so yes you can fit it in a model by itself.  The configural model would have df = 0, but adding equality constraints would still allow you to test invariance by comparing more restricted to less restricted models.

> one of the factors has an item that is best treated as continuous (V28) and the other two as ordinal (V35 and V37). I will have to see how to deal with this.

In the configural model, the continuous item's loading, intercept, and residual variance will be free across groups.  When constraining the thresholds of the 2 ordinal items to equality, just leave the continuous item as it is (free loading, intercept, and residual variance across groups).  After that, you apply constraints to loadings of all items, then intercepts of all items.  When you test residual variances for equality, you will constrain (but still estimate) the residual variance of the continuous item, whereas you must fix the residual variance of each categorical item to 1 (which is what the first group's value is fixed to for identification).

> It's strange that sometimes the full model breaks down at e.g. (thresholds + loadings) invariance but converges for the more restrictive levels. I think I'm doing the identification(s) correctly, because when the solutions converge the standard errors are computed (the routines issue warnings when an identification problem is suspected to exist).

Another reason it is a good idea to calculate your expected degrees of freedom.  You can use the formulas in Wu & Estabrook's tables to calculate your expected degrees of freedom for each model, and consult the figures to calculate the expected change in df (although I found those a little more difficult to follow than the tables).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: MLR vs MLM estimators
messages.subject_clean: MLR vs MLM estimators
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Although I haven't been able to find a source or paper to back it up, it seems like the MLM and MLR estimates produce very similar results (both in terms of standard errors and test statistics).
I have two questions how fitmeasures() in Lavaan deals with the following.

Consider the equation:

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-UktH8fgmDRs/Wr_Q9eIZ2qI/AAAAAAAAC64/bUbHwxHAdQwI2kLQ2K4ulfTMHjPTFLP_wCLcBGAs/s1600/Knipsel.PNG>

where c_t is the Satorra-Bentler scaling parameter, X²_t the chi-squared value of tested model under maximum likelihood estimation (ML) and df_t the degrees of freedom of the tested model. Those with underscore 0 (e.g. c_0) are the values of the null model.

1)
In https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00273171.2014.933697 the author recommend this kind of correction, that is: X² - c * df, rather than: X² / c - df. I am pretty sure that Lavaan provides the former (i.e. recommended) under 'CFI.robust'  and the latter under 'CFI.scaled' when using fitmeasures(.) and using estimator = 'MLM' in the fitting function (or test = 'satorra-bentler'). Is that correct?

2)
Similar to 1, when using estimator = 'MLR': is for example CFI.robust also the preferred one to use in that it is in line with the recommendations of 1)? As far as I know, the equation (as above) stays the same only the 'c' is computed differently and therefore the Yuan-Bentler test statistic and the Satorra-Bentler test statistics differ. I would like to use Yuan-Bentler one, because it can be computed with missing = 'FIML', but at the same time I would like to use the recommendations of the authors of the article that I linked. I would think, but please correct me if I am wrong, that their advice extends to the Yuan-Bentler statistic.

3) Would it make sense to use se = 'robust' together with test = 'Yuan-Bentler'? I'm asking because I am not sure if I should be using the SEs of MLM (i.e. se = 'robust') or of MLR (i.e. se = 'robust.huber.white').

Thanks in advance.

Kind regards,
Amonet

messages.body_plain:
Your second common factor, Climate, has only 2 indicators. Both loadings must be strong for the model to be identified, without additional constraints. The unstandardized loadings are 1.00 (fixed) and 0.22. The p-value on the second loading is not significant at alpha = .05. But it is also not 0 exactly. Your sample size is small. The model is " nearly not identified," as Karl Joreskog used the phrase. Like a satellite in orbit, it spins around and around the black hole if non-identification, never escapinmg but never failing outright. To establish identification, you eitehr need more constraints or more indicators on the second factor.

messages.subject_clean: Merge Predicted individual factor scores with data frame?
messages.body_plain:
How to merge Predicted individual factor scores with data frame when predicted scores are less than total observations in the original data frame?

My data frame has 10077 observations, when I run sem(), it takes into account 9745 observations. Hence, when I use lavPredict() to predict individual factor scores, there are 9745 predicted factor scores. Then, I cannot merge such 9745 scores to the 10077 obs data frame.
Here is my code:
> ctrl.labor <- "
control_labor =~ lincome+lwh+njob+skill
lincome ~~lwh
control_labor~ urbanrate+lhincome+spland_hec+owing+poor+manu_mine+uti+construction+lowser+hiser+lm1ac5+ lf_prov14+og_gov+og_busi+og_coop+og_pri+og_fdi
lincome+lwh+njob~m1ac2+major+migrated++ttnt+married+manu_mine+uti+construction+lowser+hiser+og_gov+og_busi+og_coop+og_pri+og_fdi+spland_hec
skill~lm1ac5+m1ac2+major+ttnt+married"
> fit.l <- sem(ctrl.labor, data=x180108_lkh)
> summary(fit.l, fit.measures=TRUE)
lavaan (0.5-23.1097) converged normally after 177 iterations

                                                  Used       Total
  Number of observations          9745       10077

  Estimator                                       DWLS      Robust
  Minimum Function Test Statistic              431.108     439.811
  Degrees of freedom                                19          19
  P-value (Chi-square)                           0.000       0.000
  Scaling correction factor                                  0.982
  Shift parameter                                            0.605
    for simple second-order correction (Mplus variant)
******omitted result*******

I use two ways to merge predicted values:
#This one has this error:
> newData <- cbind(x180108_lkh, lavPredict(fit.l))
Error in data.frame(..., check.names = FALSE) :
  arguments imply differing number of rows: 10077, 9745
# This one has another error:
> factorscores <- do.call(rbind, predict(fit.l, newdata = x180108_lkh))
Error in do.call(rbind, predict(fit.l, newdata = x180108_lkh)) :
  second argument must be a list

I think, overall, there is a mismatch between 10077-observations dataframe and 9745-predicted values.

I already read this post: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/lavaan/E4NPoUiKsks  and this post https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/lavaan/mf9WVimJFLY/36I-T2XbAAAJ but cannot find a solution.
Thank you very much,
Dai
